The client calls the gateway, for example GET /notes. The gateway is the client-facing intermediary: it applies the shared entrance rules and routes that request to the Notes service. Notes does the application work and reads the database. The response travels back through the gateway to the client. Sending /authors goes to Authors the same way.

Choosing Notes rather than Authors is service routing. Choosing one of the two Notes replicas is load balancing. A gateway product can do both, so the routing and the replica choice do not have to be two separate boxes. The shared policy here is an edge rule: reject an oversized body before forwarding it. Apply a bounded size check, not unlimited buffering while waiting to learn the size. Sharing that rule avoids repeating it in every service. The selected service still does the application work.

For HTTPS, method and path routing and body inspection need decrypted HTTP. TLS termination ends the client's encrypted connection at the gateway so those rules can see the request. Protect the gateway-to-service connection separately with TLS and validate the service's certificate.

Reject the oversized request at the gateway before it is forwarded. Note-specific business validation still belongs in Notes. A general entrance rule cannot decide, from application data, whether a note can be edited after it is locked.

evidence.quote: An API gateway is a client-facing intermediary that forwards API requests and applies shared entrance rules. A backend service is the application that handles the forwarded request.
The client requests /notes through the gateway. The gateway routes it to Notes, which reads the database. The response travels back through the gateway to the client.
Choosing Notes rather than Authors is service routing; distributing traffic across two Notes replicas is load balancing. A gateway product can do both, so two separate boxes are not always needed.
Use the gateway for a shared API entrance; the selected service still performs the application work.

Routing selects a destination from request properties. For example, send GET /notes to Notes and GET /authors to Authors. An edge policy is a rule at the system entrance, such as limiting request-body size before forwarding to the application.

For an HTTPS request, method/path routing and body inspection need decrypted HTTP. TLS termination means ending the client's encrypted connection at the gateway. Protect the gateway-to-service connection separately with TLS and validate the service's certificate.

In this example, reject an oversized body before forwarding it. Apply a bounded size check, not unlimited buffering while waiting to learn the body's size. Sharing the rule avoids repeating its configuration in every service.
Notes still validates note-specific rules, such as whether a note can be edited after it is locked. A general entrance rule cannot replace business decisions that depend on application data.

Authentication checks who the caller is by validating credentials. Authorization decides what that caller may do. The gateway must validate Alice's credentials. Merely receiving her token, or the header that claims she is Bob, is not validation.

The gateway must remove or replace that client-supplied identity header with the validated identity, so the claim to be Bob is not forwarded as fact. Notes can trust the forwarded identity only on a protected path that authenticates the gateway, so a caller cannot impersonate the gateway. The forwarded identity assertion must be verifiable by Notes.

The direct address has to be closed or given the same checks. Block direct external access to Notes, or enforce equivalent identity and policy checks on that path. Otherwise clients bypass the gateway. Encrypting the connection does not prove the caller is the gateway.

Notes must check permission for this particular note, using its application data. Successful gateway authentication only establishes that the caller is Alice. It is not permission to read Bob's private note. Deny that note unless Alice has permission for it.

evidence.quote: Authentication checks who the caller is by validating credentials. Authorization decides what that caller may do. The gateway validates Alice's credentials; merely receiving a token or an identity header is not validation.

Alice can send a header claiming to be Bob. Remove or replace client-supplied identity claims with the validated identity. Notes must accept that identity only through a protected path that authenticates the gateway, preventing a caller from impersonating it. Forwarded identity assertions must be verifiable by Notes.

Block direct external access to Notes, or enforce equivalent identity and policy checks on that path. Otherwise callers can bypass the gateway. Encrypting a connection alone does not prove that its caller is the gateway.
Notes checks Alice's permission for the particular note using its application data. Deny access to Bob's private note unless Alice has permission, even when gateway authentication succeeds.
Verified identity is input to the permission check, not permission to read every note.

The promised limit is a per-user quota: at most 100 accepted requests for that validated user per minute, shared by the gateway instances. Scope is which callers and which gateway instances share one allowance. A per-user limit groups requests by the validated user, and the promise is one combined allowance of 100, not 100 on each replica.

Each replica independently allowing 100 does not enforce that. If Alice's traffic is sent to both replicas, each can admit 100 and the pair can admit 200.

A burst is a short surge. A quota is an allowance over a stated period, here 100 requests per user per minute. Best-effort throttling may permit bursts or exceed a target. It is not strict quota accounting. A strict shared quota needs coordinated admission so the two replicas cannot spend the same allowance twice. That coordination adds latency, or a dependency that may require refusing work when the accounting is unavailable.

On a 429 Too Many Requests response, the client should respect any supplied retry delay, wait, and bound retries instead of repeating immediately.

Even a correctly enforced request count cannot guarantee that an expensive Notes query fits backend capacity. An expensive query costs more than a small read, and the shared database can still overload.

evidence.quote: Throttling limits request rate. A burst is a short surge; a quota is an allowance over a stated period. Scope specifies which callers and gateway instances share a limit. A per-user limit groups requests by the validated user identity.
Suppose each of two gateway replicas independently allows Alice 100 requests per minute. Sending traffic to both can admit 200. That does not enforce a promised combined allowance of 100.

Best-effort throttling may permit bursts or exceed a target; it is not strict quota accounting. A strict shared allowance needs coordinated admission so replicas cannot spend the same allowance twice. Coordination adds latency or a dependency that may require refusing work when accounting is unavailable.

On a 429 Too Many Requests response, respect any supplied retry delay; wait and bound retries instead of repeating immediately. Even a strict request-count limit cannot guarantee capacity: an expensive Notes query costs more than a small read, and a shared database can still overload.
Specify the scope and required precision before promising a limit.

The client has one two-second overall budget. The gateway's wait for Notes has to fit inside that budget, leaving time for gateway processing and for returning the response. Retry attempts and their delays spend that same remaining budget. Each attempt does not get a fresh two seconds.

The service committed the note, but the response was lost. A gateway timeout tells the client that no successful response arrived in time. It does not say whether the write committed. The outcome is unknown to the client. The timeout does not cancel the in-flight work or undo the committed note. Notes can continue after the gateway stops waiting.

If the client and the gateway can each make three total attempts, retries multiply. Three client attempts, each causing three gateway attempts, can reach Notes nine times. Retrying the creation blindly can create another note. Choose one retry owner. Here the client retries, and the gateway forwards each attempt once. Bound the attempts and delay them inside the remaining deadline.

The client reuses one idempotency key, a stable identifier for this logical create, on every attempt. Notes owns the creation effect and must enforce duplicate protection. The Notes replicas share a durable database record keyed by caller and operation ID. In one transaction, reserve that key uniquely, create the note, and record the result. Commit all or none. Concurrent repeats cannot reserve the key twice. A completed repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note.

A gateway-only key or record does not coordinate that Notes transaction, and a gateway adding a key cannot make an arbitrary write safe. A new key on every attempt describes a different operation and defeats duplicate recognition. Separate record and creation writes also leave a crash gap, so the reserve, the create, and the recorded result stay in one transaction.

evidence.quote: If the client has two seconds, the gateway's wait for Notes must fit inside that budget, leaving time for gateway processing and returning the response. Retry attempts and their delays spend the same remaining budget; each attempt does not get a fresh two seconds.

Notes may commit a new note while its response is lost. A gateway timeout or error tells the client that no successful response arrived in time, not whether the write committed. The outcome is unknown to the client.
Timing out does not by itself cancel in-flight work or undo a committed note. The service can continue after the gateway stops waiting. Retrying that creation blindly can create another note.

Retry amplification happens when layers multiply attempts. Three total client attempts, each causing three gateway attempts, can reach Notes nine times. Choose one retry owner. Here the client retries; the gateway forwards each attempt once. Bound attempts and delay them within the remaining deadline.

An idempotency key is one stable identifier for a logical operation, reused on every attempt. Deduplication means recognizing repeats. Notes, which owns the creation effect, must enforce it; a gateway adding a key cannot make an arbitrary write safe.

Notes replicas share a durable database record keyed by caller and operation ID. In one transaction, reserve that key uniquely, create the note and record the result; commit all or none. Concurrent repeats cannot reserve it twice. A completed repeat returns the recorded result without creating another note.

Separate record and creation writes leave a crash gap. A gateway-only record does not coordinate the Notes transaction. A fresh key on every retry describes different operations and defeats duplicate recognition.

Aggregation combines the Notes and Authors responses into one overview for the client. Fan-out means the gateway makes those multiple backend calls: Notes for the required notes, and Authors for the optional display names. The client makes fewer calls, which can help on a slow network. The backend work remains, and the overview now depends on more than one service. One client request is not one backend operation.

Authors is optional and is stalling. Inside a two-second overall budget, stop waiting for those names after 500 milliseconds and leave time to return the response. Return the notes that are available, and mark the display names explicitly unavailable. Do not claim the overview is complete.

If Notes fails instead, the required note data is missing. Fail the overview when that data is unavailable by its allocated deadline. Do not invent notes or disguise the loss of required data. A partial response is useful only when the missing data and the failure policy are explicit.

evidence.quote: Aggregation combines several backend responses into one client response. For a Notes overview, the gateway asks Notes for required notes and Authors for optional display names. Fan-out means making those multiple backend calls.
The client makes fewer calls, which can help on a slow network. Backend work remains, and the response now depends on multiple services. One client request does not mean one backend operation.

Choose the response contract before failure: within a two-second overall budget, for example, stop waiting for optional names after 500 milliseconds and leave time to return the response. Return available notes with names explicitly marked unavailable, rather than claiming the data is complete.

If required Notes data is unavailable by its allocated deadline, fail the overview instead. Do not invent notes or disguise required-data loss. Keep complex application workflows in a service rather than growing them inside gateway policies.
A partial response is useful only when its missing data and failure policy are explicit.

A separate gateway may be unnecessary while one adequate Notes API already checks identity, permissions, and request limits itself. There is no shared entrance across services yet, so the extra hop is not earning its cost.

Shared routing and policies across several services can justify adding one. That is the change: more than one service that should share entrance rules. The cost is a network hop, configuration, and operating responsibility.

With one gateway in front of several services, that gateway can become a common failure point. After it fails, a reachable alternate gateway must remain, and the surviving gateways and backends need enough spare capacity. Another box in the diagram is not enough.

Adding gateway replicas cannot by itself fix a saturated Notes database, because more gateways do not create database capacity. They cannot fix a bad routing rule or a failed dependency that the replicas share. They also do not supply a missing per-note permission check. Test the reachable failover path and watch latency, rejections, and backend errors before treating the shared entrance as worth its cost.

evidence.quote: One adequate Notes API can check identity, permissions and request limits itself. A separate gateway may be unnecessary. Shared routing and policies across several services can justify one, but add a network hop, configuration and operating responsibility.

The gateway can become a common failure point. Headroom is spare capacity. Surviving a gateway failure requires a reachable alternate gateway and enough surviving gateway and backend capacity, not just another box in the diagram.

Replicas can share a bad routing rule or a failed dependency. More gateways do not fix that shared failure, create capacity in a saturated Notes database or supply a missing per-note permission check.
Test the reachable failover path and watch latency, rejections and backend errors. Decide from the workload and failure behavior whether the shared entrance is worth its cost.
A gateway organizes API access; its presence alone guarantees neither security nor availability.
